charter:
# Charter — PLATFORM (standing, retrospective 2026-11-26)

**Purpose.** The standing platform every conveyor delivery project uses: the CI path and runners,
the image registry and ingress, the Postgres primary with its backups and restore, the object
store, and the shared workflows that make a build reproducible.

**Authority.** The platform owner holds the paths under the programme owner's standing delegation
(01a1ff1f-e4ba-72dc-9c1a-13049933cf14). The Architecture Board reviews the platform's standards
and its phase-G compliance. The programme board receives the platform's risks and escalations.

**Scope.** The five-node estate's shared paths and nothing above them. The platform does not own a
tenant's data model, a delivery project's plan or the programme's benefit values. A request outside
the list is a programme change.

**Standing rule.** The platform does not close. Its acceptance is the standing charter, the
approved scope baseline and a green manifest on a fresh snapshot. Each tranche review re-checks it
with the same manifest; a red manifest is a finding against the platform, not a closure trigger.

**Constraints.** No local Rust compilation; the two-run CI budget per issue; one service one
database; per-service secrets; Postgres 18 with psycopg v3; Flux as the only deployment path.

**Evidence.** The platform's record is the acceptance manifest, this pack, the docs/evidence/rework
receipt and the acts transcript. The estate's probes are the second evidence: the runner list, the
registry pull, the database recovery state, the MinIO bucket probe and the public window.

soaw.title: Statement of Architecture Work — PLATFORM standing capability (retrospective, 2026-11-26)

body.assignment: Author the standing platform's retrospective architecture record: the fifteen-artefact programme-track set, the six-section register, the delivery contract and the phase-G review, for a project that carries the programme's CI, registry, database, storage and ingress paths and does not close.
body.scope: The platform's own capabilities and their evidence, not a tenant's data model or a delivery project's plan. The record covers the five-node estate's shared paths, the standards that enforce them and the gaps that remain, with each claim traceable to a live row or a probe.
body.responsibilities: The platform owner authors and holds the record under the programme owner's delegation; the Architecture Board reviews the artefacts and the compliance level; the programme board receives the platform's risks and escalations; the delivery projects consume the paths and report a break as a platform incident.
body.acceptance_criteria: The manifest's checks pass with zero failures on a fresh snapshot, the fifteen artefacts and their documents exist, the register carries all five kinds, the delivery contract is live and the phase-G review is recorded against it, and the benefit realization records exist for every profile the programme measures.
body.contract: The delivery contract commits the platform to the charter's scope and constraints and to the evidence named here. A change to the scope or a constraint is a new statement of architecture work, not an edit to this one; the contract's supersession is recorded like any other.
body.retrospective: This statement is authored retrospectively on 2026-11-26 from the live record at snapshot 1126r and the platform plan. It records what the platform is and what it owes; it does not invent a contemporaneous history that did not exist. The delegation and the date are on the face of the record.

artifacts.body:
## Metadata

Retrospective matrix artefact for PLATFORM, authored 2026-11-26 from the live record at snapshot 1126r. The project is standing: it carries a charter, an approved scope baseline (01a1fdd8-cff3-7cd9-9535-26fed3d5836b) and the accepted deliverable 01a1ff24-a6c6-7504-a811-0fecfbc460f6, and it does not close. The programme is 01a1d039-0d24-7d16-ae52-4841e96ccfac; the project sits in tranche 0 at ADM phase Preliminary, definition plateau.

## Entries

Four groups carry the platform's work: the programme owner decides the standing charter and the tranche gates; the platform owner operates CI, runners, registry, Postgres and MinIO; the delivery projects consume the build, registry and database paths; and the Architecture Board reviews the standards and the phase-G compliance. Each row names the influence, the interest and the engagement the relationship requires, taken from the programme's roles.

## Links

The matrix derives from the platform plan docs/plans/development-process-speed.md, the programme seed's roles and the record's own approvals. Its rows are the platform's standing consumers, not a project team: the platform serves every tranche and its stakeholder set is therefore the programme's, not one delivery's.

## Document

Every group in the matrix is served by a live surface: the owner by the programme register, the delivery projects by the CI workflows and the registry, the operators by the cluster manifests and the runbooks, and the board by the published standards pack. The map is the reference the remaining PLATFORM artefacts use for their reviewers and consumers.

artifacts.body:
## Metadata

The drivers are the platform's own, recorded in docs/plans/development-process-speed.md and the programme's hard rules: CI without queueing, one build path, recoverable data and one registry. Each driver maps to a goal and an objective a tranche review can measure, so the platform is governed by outcomes rather than by infrastructure inventory.

## Entries

D1 is the 2026-11 lesson that miniature pull requests filled the org's twenty concurrent jobs; its goal is the two-run budget and its objective is read from the run log. D2 is the owner's 2026-11-20 direction that no Rust compiles on local hardware; its objective is the preflight verdict at every head. D3 and D4 are the data and image paths the estate's own rules define, each with a measurable objective.

## Links

The catalog links the platform plan, the programme's hard rules and the record's accepted deliverable. No objective depends on a metric the platform does not already emit: the CI run count comes from GitHub, the preflight verdict from the workflow, the restore evidence from the drill's receipt and the ownership count from the T0 gate.

## Document

The four rows are the platform's only standing drivers. A fifth driver would need a recorded owner decision; the catalog is deliberately small so the platform does not grow goals it cannot measure. The objectives feed the benefits diagram and the programme appraisal, which measure the same facts.

## Metadata

The requirements are the platform's standing obligations, each with a verification a reader can run against the live estate. They are not a wish list: R1–R6 are the paths every delivery project uses, so a broken one blocks a tranche rather than one project.

## Entries

R1 is the CI node's taint and runner pool; R2 is the registry's address and the CA a hand push needs; R3 is the primary and the single standby; R4 is the bare-metal MinIO unit; R5 is the ingress path behind the Cloudflare tunnels; R6 is the one-service-one-credential rule. Each row names the verification that proves it, not the configuration that assumes it.

## Links

The catalog is the reference for the platform's test and acceptance records. A requirement that cannot name a verification is not a requirement; it is removed or rewritten rather than carried as prose. The six rows are the set the platform's deliverable and the tranche reviews hold it to.

## Document

The platform's record carries the requirements as rows; its published brief cites them and its phase-G review judges against them. The catalog does not duplicate the estate's own runbooks: it states what the platform must be able to do and leaves the how to the operating procedures.

artifacts.body:
## Metadata

The concept diagram is the estate the platform owns. Five nodes, each with one job: the control plane and primary, the registry and volumes, the compute pool, the only CI node and the storage plus standby. Nothing crosses the site split invisibly: the datacenter pair and the home pair are named in the programme's infrastructure record.

## Entries

The diagram's rows are the nodes and their roles. The edges the platform cares about are the CI path from ci-1 to the registry, the registry pull on every node, the Postgres path through pgbouncer for pods and postgres.example.com for hosts, the MinIO path for object bytes and the ingress path from the Cloudflare tunnels to istio.

## Links

Every path has an owner and a probe: the runner list for CI, the CA-backed push for the registry, pg_is_in_recovery for the database, the bucket probe for MinIO and the public window probe for ingress. The diagram is the map the requirements catalog's verifications walk.

## Document

The diagram is deliberately small: a platform that needs a second CI node or a second registry is a design change with its own decision, not an extra box. The estate's five-node shape is the current answer and the programme's rules keep it singular where singularity is the requirement.

artifacts.body:
## Metadata

The capability map states what the platform does for the programme rather than what it runs. Four capabilities carry every delivery: build and verify, release, store and recover, and observe. Each names its consumers, so a capability with no consumer is visible and can be retired by decision.

## Entries

C1 is the sanctioned compile and test path: no local Rust compilation and a bounded CI budget. C2 is the image and deployment path: the one registry and Flux's reconciliation. C3 is the data path: Postgres rows, MinIO bytes and the tested restore. C4 is the observation path: the public window and the estate's health probes.

## Links

The capabilities are the vocabulary the platform's artefacts use. The requirements catalog names their verifications, the benefits diagram names their measures and the gap analysis names what is missing. No capability is claimed without a live consumer and a probe.

## Document

The map is the platform's external contract with the programme. A delivery project that needs a fifth capability is asking for a platform change, recorded as a decision and a work package rather than absorbed silently into one project's plan.

artifacts.body:
## Metadata

The catalog names the platform's four data families and the store that owns each. It is an inventory with an owner per row, not a schema: the schemas live with the application and the stores live with the platform. A data family without an owner is a finding.

## Entries

The operational rows are the record: projects, cards, runs, approvals, programme rows and the rework register, all in Postgres. The document bytes are in MinIO with tenant separation. The images are in the one registry. The secrets are per-service and never cross a service boundary, which is the platform's blast-radius rule.

## Links

Each family names its backup or restore path: the nightly dump and its offsite relay for Postgres, the MinIO bucket probe and the restore drill for bytes, the PV snapshots for the registry and the SOPS layout for secrets. The catalog is what the restore drill walks.

## Document

The catalog is the platform's data boundary. A new store is a design change; a second database user for another service is forbidden by the programme's invariants. The four families are the whole platform state, and the deliverable's evidence includes the restore path for the first.

artifacts.body:
## Metadata

The standards are the platform's enforceable choices: Postgres 18 with psycopg v3, k3s with Flux as the only deployment path, the GitHub-hosted preflight as the only Rust verdict and Leptos on wasm for the web shell. Each names the gate that enforces it, so a standard without a gate is visible.

## Entries

The database standard is the programme's own: one service, one database, one user. The delivery standard is the cluster tree Flux watches; a hand change is drift. The CI standard is the owner's 2026-11-20 direction; a local compiling cargo is denied. The web standard is the toolchain the shell actually builds with, not the host's default.

## Links

The catalog's gates are the evidence a reader can run: the migration checks, the Flux reconciliation, the preflight run and the wasm check. A standard whose gate is not wired is a finding against the platform, which is the same rule the programme applies to every project.

## Document

The standards are deliberately few and versioned. A new standard enters with a gate and an owner; an old one leaves by decision. The catalog does not list tools the platform does not enforce, because an unenforced standard is a claim the record cannot keep.

artifacts.body:
## Metadata

The gap matrix states what the platform cannot yet prove. It is a work list, not an accusation: each row names the baseline, the target and the work package that closes it. The platform is standing, so its gaps are closed tranche by tranche rather than at one closure.

## Entries

The first gap is the 2026-11 CI lesson: miniature pull requests cost ninety-one and sixty-one runs on two tickets, and the fix is the lane protocol plus the hosted preflight. The second is the standby's untested promotion. The third is the registry's CA step. The fourth is the deliberate CI exemption for the heavy-GPU bare-metal services, where the device test is the gate.

## Links

Each gap names the artefact or work package that closes it: the budget rule in the lane protocol, the drill's receipt, the registry runbook and the device deploy-test. A gap without a work package is not in the matrix; it is a risk in the register.

## Document

The matrix is the platform's honest distance from its target. It is updated at every tranche review, and a gap that survives two reviews without a work package is escalated to the programme board rather than carried indefinitely.

artifacts.body:
## Metadata

The catalog records the platform's choices with their criteria, including doing nothing. It is short because the platform's shape is deliberately singular: one CI node, one registry, one primary. The rejected options are recorded so a later session does not re-open a settled decision as a fresh idea.

## Entries

S1 is the owner's 2026-11-20 direction: the compile verdict comes from the hosted preflight, not from a local cargo. S2 is the cluster's own runner pool for the service workflows. S3 was rejected because a second CI node doubles the failure surface without addressing the queue's cause, which was too many miniature PRs. S0 was rejected on the measured waste and the direction.

## Links

The criteria are the platform's own: no local compilation, no queue behind miniature units, one failure model and a measurable budget. An option that fails a criterion is recorded as rejected rather than silently dropped; the record is the argument the next session reads.

## Document

The chosen options are the platform's live shape. The rejected ones are decisions with their reasons, not open questions. A reversal needs a new decision and this catalogue keeps the old one visible so the reversal is explicit.

artifacts.body:
## Metadata

The context diagram places the platform between the programme it serves and the external services it uses. The programme is the conveyor buildout; the estate is the five nodes; the externals are GitHub for source and CI, Cloudflare for the public window and the tailnet for private transport; the tenants are nonagentic, AHTAPol and w2v.

## Entries

The diagram's rows are relationships, not boxes: the programme is served, GitHub is depended on in both directions, the network is exposed through two paths, and the tenants are served under separate boundaries. The tenant boundary is the platform's licensing and isolation rule, not a deployment detail.

## Links

Each relationship has a failure mode the platform owns: a GitHub outage stops merges and preflight; a Cloudflare outage closes the public window; a tailnet fault splits the sites; and a tenant boundary breach is the one failure the platform must never allow. The diagram is the map the platform's incident procedures use.

## Document

The context is stable across tranches, which is why it is a platform artefact rather than a project one. A new external service or a new tenant is a context change with a decision, and the diagram is updated with the decision rather than after it.

artifacts.body:
## Metadata

The benefits diagram connects the platform's goals to the programme's benefit profiles. The programme KPI is the owner's 2026-11-26 decision: deliver programmes at quality with the least rework; cost is not a factor yet. The diagram names the measures the platform actually emits, not aspirational metrics.

## Entries

G1 is the KPI and its measure is the rework register: open packages per accepted deliverable. B1 is evidenced by the approval-decision row count, B2 by the tool_call ledger, B6 by the register findings. The platform provides the environment these measures run in; the programme's benefit profiles own the values.

## Links

The diagram links each measure to its instrument: the rework register, the approval and tool_call tables, the coverage and register checks. A benefit whose measure has no instrument is not on the diagram; it is a kata candidate in the register.

## Document

The diagram is the platform's contribution to the programme's benefit realisation. It does not claim realisation: the transition records own the baseline and the post readings, and the platform's role is the environment and the measures that make them possible.

artifacts.body:
## Metadata

The plan catalog sequences the platform's four work packages and the estate's migration path. The packages are live; what remains is the evidence: the restore drill, the shared workflow consumption and the tranche-by-tranche confirmation that the platform still serves.

## Entries

The work packages are the platform's standing units: CI and runners, registry and ingress, Postgres with backups and restore, and the shared workflows and archetypes. Their tranche is 0 because the platform exists before the delivery tranches; their state is live and the catalog records the evidence each still owes.

## Links

The migration path is the estate's, not the platform's: the five nodes are the target and the retired nodes are gone. The plan records the path's decision points — the site split, the standby, the registry move — so a later reader can see why the estate looks as it does.

## Document

The catalog is the platform's plan of record. It is updated at each tranche review with the state of the four packages; a package that regresses reopens as a gap rather than silently staying green.

artifacts.body:
## Metadata

The review catalog records the platform's compliance history. The 2026-11-22 review judged the platform non_conformant against its then contract; this rework records a fresh phase-G review against the delivery contract it authors, with the evidence the review reads. The history is kept so the improvement is visible.

## Entries

The catalog's rows are the reviews and their levels. A review is recorded against a live contract and cites the delegation, the manifest and the acceptance record. The platform is standing, so its reviews are periodic rather than closure-driven; the catalog is the series.

## Links

The levels are the six the architecture standard defines. A non_conformant review is not erased by a later compliant one; it is the earlier state, and the catalog keeps both so the trajectory is readable. A waiver would be recorded with its accepting owner and date.

## Document

The catalog is the platform's governance memory. The phase-G review this pack records is the current verdict; the earlier one is the baseline it improved from. Both are rows, and the published standards pack renders them from the record.

artifacts.body:
## Metadata

The change catalog records the architecture changes the rework made, each with its authorisation. It is a retrospective change record: the changes landed on the #526 lane under the owner's delegation, and the catalog names them so the platform's standards history is explicit rather than inferred from a diff.

## Entries

The first change is the action-registry projection: the snapshot now writes actions.json, so the blueprint's Action registry section resolves from the served registry rather than from a design-pack copy. The second is the five ADR-kind decision records that carry the licensing frame, the blueprint states, the options and programme appraisals and the solution intent. The third is the standards corrections.

## Links

Each change is authorised by the #526 delegation and recorded against its work package. A change without an authorisation is not in the catalog; it is a finding against the platform. The catalog is the bridge between the rework's acts and the standards' history.

## Document

## Entries

AR2 comes from the action registry, verified by the projection and the audit. AR3 comes from SPEC_V2 §8.3, verified by the benefit lifecycle tests. AR4 comes from TOGAF and D63, verified by the contract and phase gates.

documents.body:
# Project Brief — PLATFORM

## Outcome

The platform is the standing capability every conveyor delivery project uses: the CI path and
runners, the image registry and ingress, the Postgres primary with its backups and restore, and
the shared workflows that make a build reproducible. Its outcome is not a closure: the platform
stays live for the programme's whole life and its acceptance is the standing charter plus the
evidence that each path works. This rework records that evidence.

## Boundary

The platform owns the five-node estate's shared paths and nothing above them. It does not own a
tenant's data model, a delivery project's plan or the programme's benefit values. It owns the
cluster, the registry, the database primary and standby, the object store, the ingress and the CI
runners. A request outside that list is a programme change, not a platform task.

## Reuse sources

The platform's plan is docs/plans/development-process-speed.md, the 2026-11-10 audit of the Rust
development process. The programme's hard rules supply the invariants: one service one database,
per-service secrets, no local Rust compilation, the two-run CI budget. The estate's infrastructure
record supplies the node names, the endpoints and the credentials layout.

## Inception units

The platform's work packages are CI and runners, registry and ingress, Postgres with backups and
restore, and the shared workflows and archetypes. Each was delivered before the delivery tranches
and each owes evidence at this review: a green preflight, a registry pull, a restore receipt and a
consuming workflow. The four units are the platform's standing work list.

## Dependencies

public window; on the tailnet for transport; and on the estate's power and network for both sites.
Every delivery project depends on the platform, so a platform outage is a programme outage rather
than one project's risk. The dependency is recorded in both directions.

## Acceptance

approved, its deliverable is accepted with demo credit, and its manifest's checks are green. This
rework adds the artefact standard, the register and the phase-G review; the acceptance does not
close the project. A later tranche review re-checks the platform with the same manifest.

## Capabilities

has a live consumer and a probe: the preflight at every head, the registry pull on every node, the
restore drill, and the public window plus the estate's health probes. The capabilities are the
platform's external contract with the programme.

## Plan

confirmation that the paths still work. The platform's next steps are the restore drill, the
shared-workflow consumption and the observation path's evidence. Each lands as a work package
under the standing charter rather than a new project.

documents.title: Evidence — PLATFORM (retrospective, 2026-11-26)
documents.body:
# Evidence — PLATFORM

## Claim

The standing platform's paths are live and its record is conformant: the CI node runs the
sanctioned preflight, the registry serves the images, the Postgres primary and its standby answer,
MinIO holds the bytes, the ingress carries the public window, and the platform's charter, baseline,
artefacts, register and phase-G review exist as rows with evidence.

## Evidence

The record's own rows: the charter asset, the approved scope baseline, the accepted deliverable
with its demo credit, the five WBS nodes, the six-section register and the phase-G review against
the delivery contract. The estate's probes: the runner list, the registry pull, the database's
recovery state, the MinIO bucket probe and the public window. The acceptance manifest at
acceptance/programme/PLATFORM.toml names the executable checks.

## Verification

Run `python3 scripts/verify-project.py --project PLATFORM --snapshot <fresh>` and read the receipt:
every check must pass with zero failures on a snapshot taken after the writes. Run the estate
probes named in the requirements catalog; a probe that cannot run is a gap, not a pass. The
phase-G review reads the contract, the scope baseline and the delegation.

## Links

The deliverable's evidence list names this file, the acceptance manifest and the acts record. The
artefacts link to the requirements, the benefits diagram and the change catalog. The register's
rows link to the decisions they depend on. Every link resolves at the snapshot's git sha.

## Gap

The gaps the platform still carries are the restore drill, the standby promotion and the
heavy-GPU services' device deploy-test. They are recorded in the gap matrix and the register; none
is claimed as done. The platform is green when its manifest passes, not when its gaps disappear —
the gaps are the programme's work, tracked where a later review can see them.

documents.title: Gap Analysis — PLATFORM (retrospective, 2026-11-26)
documents.body:
# Gap Analysis — PLATFORM

## Baseline

The baseline is the platform as the record measured it before this rework: a live charter and
scope baseline, an accepted deliverable, but no artefacts, no six-section register, no phase-G
review against a delivery contract and a red mandatory artefact standard. The earlier compliance
review judged the platform non_conformant against its statement of architecture work.

## Target

The target is the standing platform with the full programme-track artefact set, the register, the
delivery contract and the phase-G review, its manifest green on a fresh snapshot, and its known
gaps recorded as work rather than hidden as passes. The platform stays active; the target is
conformance, not closure.

## Gaps and work packages

Four gaps remain after the rework: the restore drill, the standby promotion, the registry push's
CA step and the heavy-GPU device deploy-test. The rework closes the record gaps — the artefacts,
the register, the contract, the review and the benefit realization records — and records the
operational gaps with their owners and review dates. A gap without a work package is a risk in
the register, not an unrecorded absence.

documents.title: Candidate Solutions — PLATFORM (retrospective, 2026-11-26)
documents.body:
# Candidate Solutions — PLATFORM

## Candidates

Three candidates for the platform's CI and delivery shape: the GitHub-hosted preflight as the
only Rust verdict; the cluster's own ARC runners for the service workflows; and the one-registry,
Flux-only delivery path. Each candidate names the path it serves and the failure it prevents.

## Criteria

The criteria are the owner's directions and the measured lessons: no local Rust compilation, a
bounded CI budget, one failure model per shared path, and a verification a reader can run. A
candidate that cannot name its verification is not a candidate; it is a wish.

## Options rejected

A second CI node was rejected because it doubles the failure surface without addressing the queue,
whose cause was miniature pull requests rather than capacity. Keeping the local compilation was
rejected on the owner's direction and the measured 91 and 61 runs two tickets consumed. Doing
nothing was rejected because the programme's own tranches depend on the platform's paths.

documents.title: Project Context Diagram — PLATFORM (retrospective, 2026-11-26)
documents.body:
# Project Context Diagram — PLATFORM

## Context

The platform sits between the conveyor programme and the services it depends on: GitHub for
source and CI, Cloudflare for the public window, the tailnet for private transport, and the
estate's two sites for its nodes. The programme is its consumer; the services are its suppliers.

## Affected organisation

The programme owner decides the platform's charter and the tranche gates; the platform owner
operates the paths; the delivery projects consume them; the Architecture Board reviews the
standards. The platform's incidents reach the programme board through the register's escalations,
not through an informal channel.

## Affected systems

The five nodes and their roles: the control plane and Postgres primary, the registry and volumes,
the compute pool, the only CI node, and MinIO with the standby. The external systems are GitHub,
Cloudflare and the tailnet. A change to any of them is a platform change with a decision and a
record, not a local adjustment.

documents.title: Benefits Diagram — PLATFORM (retrospective, 2026-11-26)
documents.body:
# Benefits Diagram — PLATFORM

## Goals and outcomes

The platform's goal is the programme KPI the owner set on 2026-11-26: deliver programmes at
quality with the least amount of rework. Cost is not a factor yet; the platform's outcome is a
build-and-deliver path that does not itself create rework through queues, drift or untested
recovery.

## Measures

The measures are the rework register's open packages per accepted deliverable, the CI runs per
issue against the two-run budget, the preflight verdict at every pushed head, the restore drill's
receipt and the public window's probe. Each measure has an instrument in the record; none is a
stored opinion.

## Benefits and sub-benefits

The platform evidences B1 (the decision ladder's rows), B2 (the tool_call ledger), B5 (the one
ownership matrix) and B6 (the record agreeing with itself). It enables the other profiles without
owning their values. The benefits diagram links each measure to the benefit profile that owns it,
and the transition records carry the baseline and post readings.

# Architecture Artefact Index — PLATFORM

## Metadata

This index names the fifteen typed artefacts the platform's programme-track architecture set
carries, their phases and plateaus, and the document that publishes each. It is the entry point
the Architecture Board reads before the artefacts themselves; the artefacts are the rows, the
index is their map.

## Entries

The set runs from Phase A's stakeholder map, driver catalog, requirements catalog and solution
concept diagram through Phase B's capability map, Phase C's data catalog and Phase D's technology
standards, then Phase E's gap matrix, candidate solutions, context diagram and benefits diagram,
Phase F's migration plan, Phase G's compliance review catalog and Phase H's change and
requirement catalogs. Each entry names its artefact row and its published document.

## Links

Every artefact links to at least one other: the requirements to the drivers, the capability map to
the solution concept, the gap matrix to the capability map and standards, the migration plan to
the candidates, standards, gaps and benefits, and the Phase H catalogs to the reviews and the
requirements. The graph is the derivation the board inspects.

## Document

The index is itself an artefact document: the published body the architecture repository reads
alongside the typed rows. A reader who needs the platform's architecture starts here and follows
the links; a reader who needs one artefact reads its own document. The index never duplicates an
artefact's content, it points.

documents.title: Safe Art — PLATFORM (retrospective, 2026-11-26)
documents.body:
# Safe Art — PLATFORM

## ART charter

The ART is the programme's delivery rhythm: a PI per tranche, a refinement before it, a retro
after it, and the demo credit on each accepted deliverable. Its authority is the programme
owner's standing delegation and its scope is the programme's projects, not a tenant's product.
The charter names the ART's outcomes so a review can judge them.

## Solution intent

The ART intends a programme that delivers at quality with the least rework: tranche 0 green with
its seven members evidenced, tranches 1–4 reworked in order, the benefit realization records
written, and the public pack carrying the current record. The intent's constraints are the
owner's directions and the estate's rules, which the deliverable's evidence cites.

## Backlog with WSJF

The backlog is the programme's accepted deliverables, each carrying the four WSJF inputs the PI
plan records. The platform's own deliverable scores business value 5, time criticality 5, risk
reduction 3 and job size 6; the ordering is the programme's, and a deliverable without its four
inputs is not on the backlog.

## Shared configuration

The programme's shared configuration carries the cadence, the job-family pins, the default
approval policy and the knowledge pins its projects inherit. It is a real row, written through
`programmes.update`; an empty object is absence, not a configuration, and the standard treats it
that way.

documents.title: Inspect and Adapt — PLATFORM (retrospective, 2026-11-26)
documents.body:
# Inspect and Adapt — PLATFORM

## What went well

The platform's paths held through the rework: the hosted preflight gave a compile verdict at
every pushed head, the registry served the images, the Postgres primary and its standby answered,
and the record's own artifacts could be authored from the live rows. The rework's factory resumed
across four blocked attempts without duplicating a single row.

## What did not

Three defects surfaced only by running: the governed-asset vocabulary lagged the database CHECK
by ten kinds and made the first list a 500; the plan's work packages predated the card
requirement and their update was refused; and two pre-existing change rows carried no approved
gate, so the WBS guard refused them. Each is now a fix with a test or a constraint behind it.

## Lessons

The durable lesson is that the record's vocabulary and its database must be one list, and that a
guard which reads an approval link needs the action that creates it to write that link. Both are
recorded as programme lessons and one is a kata candidate; the kata is the mechanism that keeps a
future session from rediscovering them.

## Actions

The three defects are fixed on the lane, each with its own evidence. The platform's remaining
actions are the restore drill, the standby promotion and the shared-workflow consumption, all
recorded in the gap matrix and the register with owners and review dates.

## Kata candidates

`L-PLATFORM-1` is the kata candidate: keep the domain enum identical to the database CHECK, and
make a list action that parses every stored row the test that proves it. The signature is
`enum-mirrors-check`; the lesson is evidenced by the #526 issue, the PLATFORM receipt and the
factory's change.

risk.title: The platform's dependency on a single CI node is a single point of failure for every tranche
risk.body: ci-1 is the only CI node in the cluster; the hosted preflight carries the Rust verdict, but every service workflow still depends on ci-1's runner pool. A loss of ci-1 stalls the cluster-local CI path until the node returns or the workflows move. The risk is recorded, not waived: the hosted preflight is the fallback and the queue's cause has been addressed by the CI budget.

risk.body: The Postgres standby on storage-1 is live and answers as a replica; no promotion has been exercised end to end. The nightly dump and its offsite relay exist, but a restore receipt from a real promotion is the evidence the platform owes. The risk is a gap in the gap matrix and a row here until the drill's receipt is published.

meta.owner: the platform owner under the #526 rework delegation

issue.title: The live public window lags the committed pack until the next publish
issue.body: The committed design pack can be ahead of the deployed snapshot between publishes. The rework's publish step closes the gap; until it runs, a reader of the public site sees the previous state. The issue is recorded against this rework and closed by the publish, not by hand-editing the pack.

assumption.title: The replay record is the programme's working record until the rework is promoted
assumption.body: The rework writes through the product's actions against the replay base rebuilt from the production dump on 2026-11-26. The assumption is that the replay is the record of work until the promotion unit replays these acts into the live database; if it is not, the receipts prove a copy rather than the programme. The assumption is recorded so the promotion unit can discharge it.

dependency.title: Every delivery tranche depends on the platform's CI, registry and Postgres paths
dependency.body: A delivery project's build, image and database path all run through the platform. This row records that tranches 1–13 depend on the platform's four work packages remaining live and its endpoints stable; a platform change that breaks a path blocks a tranche rather than one project.

benefit.title: B1 Auditable decisions: every choice has a decision row
benefit.body: The benefit profile 01a1e9de-4e4f-757e-a8c8-bf3522e5adcf records B1 Auditable decisions, measured at 0.15861 approval decisions per run on 2026-11-22. This retrospective row links the platform's contribution — the decision ladder's live path — to the profile without claiming realisation; the transition record carries the baseline and the readiness.

body.commitments: The platform commits to the four capabilities — build and verify, release, store and recover, and observe — each with a live probe, and to the constraints that keep them singular: one CI node, one registry, one primary and one ownership home.
body.compliance: Compliance is judged at phase G against this contract: the charter, the baseline, the artefacts, the register and the review must exist and be consistent. The earlier non_conformant review is the baseline; this rework's review is the current verdict.
body.approval: The contract is approved by the Architecture Board under the programme owner's standing delegation 01a1ff1f-e4ba-72dc-9c1a-13049933cf14. The approval is a recorded decision, not a signature on a document.
body.capacity: The platform's capacity is the five-node estate: ci-1's runner pool for CI, registry-1's registry and volumes, deploy-host's control plane and primary, compute-1's compute and storage-1's storage and standby. A capacity change is an estate change with its own decision.
body.acceptance: Acceptance is the manifest's checks passing on a fresh snapshot, with the standing rule that the platform does not close. The deliverable accepted with demo credit is the standing record itself; a later review re-checks it with the same checks.
body.evidence: The evidence is this pack, the acceptance manifest, the rework receipt, the acts transcript and the estate's probes. A claim in this contract that the evidence does not support is a finding against the platform, not a wording issue.
body.retrospective: Authored 2026-11-26 from the live record; the contract records the standing obligation rather than a one-off delivery.

The charter is approved, the scope baseline is approved, the fifteen artefacts and their documents exist, the register carries all five kinds, and the benefit realization records exist. The earlier 2026-11-22 review's non_conformant level is kept in the review catalog as the baseline this rework improved from; no waiver is claimed.

assets.title: Licensing frame
assets.body:
# Licensing frame — conveyor programme

The conveyor's own publishing is public: the design pack at conveyor.nonagentic.ai/design/ is
the programme's public site, its standards pack is public, and its issues are public. The
tenant-facing application is opt-in: a tenant is provisioned, its rows are tenant-scoped, and its
users reach only their tenant's data through the authentication realm that admits them. The
boundary is the tenant: no view crosses it, no inference call carries another tenant's data, and
no shared cache holds a tenant's bytes without its key.

The licence-gated applications in the estate are separate products with their own realms and
their own licence checks; the conveyor does not carry their licence tokens and does not resell
their capabilities. A tool the conveyor calls is either the conveyor's own, a tenant's OpenAPI or
MCP toolkit under the tenant's credentials, or a platform service the estate operates. There is no
third-party licence inside the conveyor's own runtime.

The frame is a decision record, adopted 2026-11-26 as part of the #526 rework. It is the source
the business case's Licensing frame section cites, and a change to it is a new decision, not an
edit to this record.

assets.title: Blueprint states
assets.body:
# Blueprint states — current, intermediate and target

The current state is the V1 work system with the V2 organisational model added around it: the
work hierarchy, the catalogue, the decision ladder and the programme record exist as rows, the
web shell carries the §10.5 destinations as real routes, and the programme's TOGAF/SAFe/PMP/MSP
artefacts are published. Its weak point is proof: many projects' records were closed on red
manifests or reconstructed after the fact, which is the rework's subject.

The intermediate state is the retrospective rework: tranche 0 completed with every member green,
then tranches 1–4 reworked in programme order, each project's artefacts, register, contract and
review authored from the facts, and the public pack republished after each batch. In the
intermediate state the programme's own KPI is measurable: open rework packages per accepted
deliverable fall tranche by tranche.

The target state is the programme closed with every tranche reviewed, every benefit's transition
recorded with a post reading, and the rework register empty of P0/P1 packages. The conveyor is then
an organisation that works the conveyor: the self-development loop, the operations loop and the
programme loop each have live evidence. The target is a direction, not a date; the programme's
tranche reviews judge progress toward it.

Adopted 2026-11-26 as a decision record under the #526 rework delegation.

assets.title: Options appraisal
assets.body:
# Options appraisal — the V2 destinations

The question is how the V2 §10.5 destinations reach the live product. Option A keeps the V1
nine-destination shell and renders the V2 pages only in the design pack; it is rejected because
D64 makes the app the real UI and a mock page is evidence of intent, never of implementation.
Option B adds the V2 destinations as routes in the existing shell, around the V1 routes, each
with its Playwright spec; it is chosen because it preserves the working V1 surface and makes every
destination reachable and tested.

Option C rewrites the shell as a new application; it is rejected because the rewrite would
duplicate the V1 routes and delay the programme for a shell change that is not the bottleneck.
Doing nothing is the fourth option and is rejected for the same reason as A: the acceptance
finding stays red and the destinations remain API-only.

The appraisal is qualitative on cost and decisive on the record: option B is the one the code
already implements, with the routes and six e2e specs live. Adopted 2026-11-26 as a decision
record under the #526 rework delegation; its evidence is the app's route table and the specs.

assets.title: Programme appraisal
assets.body:
# Programme appraisal — quality with the least rework

The programme's KPI, set by the owner on 2026-11-26, is to deliver programmes at quality with the
least amount of rework. Cost is not a factor yet: the first job is to make the programme able to
work. This record replaces the money investment appraisal the MSP template's heading originally
asked for; an NPV or cash-flow schedule would be invented, and an invented appraisal is worse than
an honest measure.

The measure is rework packages per accepted deliverable. At the 2026-11-26 record the rework
register carries the programme's open packages and the demo credits carry the accepted
deliverables; the ratio is the programme's own rework rate. The baseline is taken from the live
register at this snapshot; the target is a falling rate, tending to zero as the tranches complete,
and the tranche reviews report it.

The appraisal's basis is the register and the snapshot, both public and reproducible. Its
cost posture is stated, not modelled: the inference ledger meters tokens and cost per call, the
platform's infrastructure is the estate's, and no money budget is asserted while the rework runs.
When the programme works, a cost appraisal can be added as a new decision; until then this is the
programme's appraisal.

Adopted 2026-11-26 as a decision record under the #526 rework delegation.

assets.title: Solution intent
assets.body:
# Solution intent — the programme ART

The ART's intended outcomes are the programme's: tranche 0 green with all seven members evidenced,
tranches 1–4 reworked in programme order, the benefit realization records written with their
baselines and readiness, and the public pack carrying the current record after every batch. The
intent is stated as outcomes because the ART's job is the programme's delivery, not a component's.

The measures are the tranche reviews' exit checks, the rework register's package count, the
benefit profiles' baselines and post readings, and the publish gates. Each is a row or a
reproducible check; none is a stored opinion. The ART's cadence is the programme's own: a PI per
tranche, a refinement before it, a retro after it, and the demo credit on the accepted
deliverable.

The constraints are the owner's directions and the estate's rules: no local Rust compilation, a
two-run CI budget per issue, Postgres 18 with psycopg v3, one service one database, per-service
secrets, and the programme's tranche gate that refuses a start before authorisation. The intent is
satisfied when the constraints hold and the outcomes are evidenced, not when a plan says so.

Adopted 2026-11-26 as a decision record under the #526 rework delegation.
